Region Selection

region-selection.Rmd

Introduction

stGradient provides two approaches for defining regions of interest (ROIs):

  1. Interactive selection via the Shiny app
  2. Automated detection using DBSCAN clustering

Launching the Interactive Polygon Selector

The Shiny app allows you to interactively draw polygons on spatial data to define ROIs:

launch_stGradient()

Workflow in the App

  1. Enter your Seurat object name — the name of the object in your R session
  2. Enter FOV name — the field of view name (typically "fov")
  3. Click “Load Data” — loads cell coordinates and plots them
  4. Draw polygons — use the freehand drawing toolbar on the plot
  5. Enter polygon object name — name for the extracted polygon object
  6. Click “Extract Polygons” — saves polygons to your global environment

The resulting polygon object is an sf object that can be passed directly to downstream stGradient functions.

DBSCAN-Based Polygon Detection

The add_dbscan_polygons() function automatically identifies ROIs by clustering cancer-labeled cells using the DBSCAN algorithm, then wrapping detected clusters in concave hull polygons.

Using Known DBSCAN Parameters

If you already have starting values for eps and minPts (for example, from a previous sample on the same platform), pass them directly:

library(stGradient)

seurat_obj <- add_dbscan_polygons(
  seurat_obj,
  eps = 35,         # neighborhood radius (microns)
  minPts = 20,      # minimum cluster size
  concavity = 2     # concave hull tightness (lower = tighter)
)

# Access the polygon object
auto_polygons <- get_cancer_regions(seurat_obj)

Choosing Parameters Without Priors

If you don’t have prior values, you can optimize them from the data in three steps:

  1. Grid search. optimize_dbscan_params() runs DBSCAN on the cancer cells for every combination of eps and minPts in a grid and scores each combination by silhouette score, which measures how well separated the clusters are.
  2. Filter out noisy settings. DBSCAN labels a cancer cell as noise when it is not part of, or within eps of, a dense core (a cell with at least minPts neighbors within eps). Noise cells are not assigned to any cluster, so they fall outside every polygon. noise_pct is the fraction of cancer cells labeled noise. Settings with a high noise_pct miss many cancer cells, so only candidates below the noise_pct cutoff (default 15%) are scored further.
  3. Compare coverage and purity. For each remaining candidate, polygons are built and scored by cancer_covered (fraction of cancer cells that fall inside a polygon) and purity (fraction of cells inside polygons that are cancer). Larger eps or smaller minPts tends to raise coverage but pulls in more non-cancer cells, lowering purity. fbeta combines both into one score; with b = 0.5, purity counts more than coverage.

Optimizing DBSCAN Parameters

optimize_dbscan_params() runs all three steps in one call. noise_pct sets the maximum fraction of cancer cells labeled noise for a combination to be scored, b sets the F-beta weighting, and plot = TRUE draws coverage, purity and F-beta heatmaps, with the best combination outlined in red on the F-beta heatmap. Results are sorted by fbeta, so the best combination is in the first row:

results <- optimize_dbscan_params(
  seurat_obj,
  noise_pct = 0.15,  # keep combinations with < 15% of cancer cells as noise
  b = 0.5,           # weight purity more than coverage
  plot = TRUE        # draw coverage, purity and F-beta heatmaps
)

# View top parameter combinations
head(results)

# Use the best parameters
best <- results[1, ]
seurat_obj <- add_dbscan_polygons(seurat_obj, eps = best$eps, minPts = best$minPts)

The returned data frame has one row per eps/minPts combination with sil_score, n_clusters, noise_pct, n_regions, cancer_covered, purity and fbeta. Combinations above the noise_pct cutoff have NA for the coverage, purity and fbeta columns. The heatmaps are also stored in attr(results, "plot") for saving.

You can customize the search ranges:

results <- optimize_dbscan_params(
  seurat_obj,
  noise_pct = 0.15,
  b = 0.5,
  plot = TRUE,
  eps_range = seq(20, 80, by = 10),
  minPts_range = c(15, 20, 30, 50),
  max_sample = 30000  # reduce for faster computation
)

Visualizing Detected Polygons

Use plot_dbscan_polygons() to inspect the results before proceeding:

# Plot with polygons overlaid
plot_dbscan_polygons(seurat_obj)

# Get polygons without plotting (useful for pipelines)
auto_polygons <- plot_dbscan_polygons(seurat_obj, plot = FALSE)

Adding Polygon Membership

Once you have polygons (from either the Shiny app or DBSCAN), annotate each cell as inside or outside:

# Add inside/outside metadata column
seurat_obj <- add_polygon_membership(seurat_obj, auto_polygons)

This adds an inside_polygon column to seurat_obj@meta.data with logical values.

QC Visualization

After assigning membership, use qc_plot_xenium() to visualize the spatial layout:

qc_out <- qc_plot_xenium(
  obj = seurat_obj,
  roi_col = "inside_polygon",
  celltype_col = "first_type",
  show = "both",
  zoom = TRUE,
  zoom_pad = 0.05,
  grey_outside_roi = TRUE
)

ROI Composition Plots

Examine cell type distributions inside vs. outside the region:

# Distribution inside ROI only
plot_roi_celltype_dist(
  df = qc_out$df,
  roi_col = "inside_polygon",
  celltype_col = "first_type",
  metric = "proportion"
)

# Stacked inside vs outside
plot_roi_inout_celltype_stack(
  df = qc_out$df,
  roi_col = "inside_polygon",
  celltype_col = "first_type"
)

#Dodged inside vs outside
plot_roi_inout_celltype_dodge(
  df = qc_out$df,
  roi_col = "inside_polygon",
  celltype_col = "first_type",
  metric = "count",
  top_n = 10
)
